narr: Welcome to this course on the History of Uzbekistan. In this video, we'll explore weeks 5 and 6 of your studies.
This is a compulsory module worth 4 ECTS credits, offered by the Tashkent University of Technology's Faculty of Energy.
The course consists of 30 contact hours of lectures plus 90 hours of independent work, totaling 120 hours.
Assessment includes a midterm exam worth 30%, a project presentation worth 20%, and a final exam worth 50%.
To pass, you'll need a minimum of 75% attendance to be admitted to the final exam.
The grading scale ranges from A for excellent to D for unsatisfactory.

data.heading: Intended Learning Outcomes
bullets: Understanding — explain basic concepts of history, statehood, and the role of science and technology
Analysis — analyze contemporary Uzbek politics in retrospect
Selection — select qualitative and quantitative data and methods
Evaluation — judge political changes and reforms

narr: There are five intended learning outcomes for this course.
First, you'll develop an understanding of basic historical concepts and the role of science and technology.
Second, you'll learn to analyze contemporary Uzbek politics with historical perspective.
Third, you'll master selecting appropriate qualitative and quantitative data and methods.
Fourth, you'll be able to evaluate political changes and reforms.
Finally, you'll apply your knowledge by working on group projects and presenting historical processes.
This manual covers weeks 5 and 6, focusing on two main thematic blocks.
The first block is 'National Legislation and Judicial Systems', covering the creation of the 1992 Constitution and the history of criminal courts.
The second block addresses 'Human Rights and Elimination of Forced Labor', including ILO conventions and national labor legislation.
All facts, dates, and figures are taken from scientific articles, with quotes given in Russian translation.
To use this manual effectively, start with the 'Key Points' section for each week.
Then solve the open questions aloud, take the tests, learn the glossary terms, and review the 'Cheat Sheet' before exams.

narr: Week 5 focuses on National Legislation and Judicial Systems with four assigned articles.
These articles cover the creation of Uzbekistan's Constitution, the development of criminal courts, the judicial system during World War II, and the stages of legal system development.
Week 6 addresses Human Rights and Elimination of Forced Labor with two articles.
These articles discuss the abolition of forced labor in Uzbekistan and forced child labor in the cotton industry.
All six articles are scientific publications from 2013 to 2024, forming the basis for questions, tests, and terms in this course.
Week 5 addresses several important questions about Uzbekistan's legal history.
We'll explore how the first Constitution of independent Uzbekistan was created in 1992.
We'll examine the development of criminal courts from ancient times to the present.
We'll study how the judicial system functioned in the Uzbek SSR during 1939-1945.
Finally, we'll analyze the four stages of legal system development in independent Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Key Provisions: Creation of the Constitution
bullets: The idea of a new Constitution emerged with the Declaration of Independence on June 20, 1990
A Constitutional Commission of 64 people was created, headed by President I.A. Karimov
In 1992, the commission was expanded to 71 members
Working groups were formed to draft different sections of the Constitution
Constitutions of several countries were studied as references
The concept of the President's rule of law was adopted as the basis

narr: Let's begin with the key provisions about the creation of Uzbekistan's Constitution.
The idea for a new Constitution emerged alongside the Declaration of Independence in June 1990.
A Constitutional Commission of 64 people was established, led by President I.A. Karimov.
The commission was later expanded to 71 members in July-August 1992.
Working groups were formed to draft different sections including the preamble, rights and obligations, and state structure.
The drafters studied constitutions from various countries including the USA, Germany, France, and others.
Among alternative concepts, the President's rule of law was chosen as the foundation for the new Constitution.

data.heading: Versions of the Draft Constitution
bullets: Initially drafted in Russian, then translated into Uzbek
Each version was personally reviewed by the President

narr: The Constitution went through several versions before its final adoption.
The first version was ready by October-November 1991, containing 158 articles across six sections.
In spring 1992, a second version reduced this to 149 articles.
This was followed by a third version with 137 articles.
For nationwide discussion, a text of 127 articles was published.
The draft was initially compiled in Russian and later translated into Uzbek.
Each version was personally reviewed by President Karimov before proceeding to the next.
